title: Why influencers are rejecting the tradwife label
description:
Tradwife content is everywhere - you’ve seen it on your feed. Influencers showing off their sourdough loaves while talking about how lucky they are to be stay-at-home wives, mothers, and girlfriends. For some, it looks like an aspirational lifestyle - fairy-tale wealth, a beautiful home, family and no 9-5 job.

One of the biggest accounts like this is Nara Smith. And although she’s often seen as the face of the movement, she’s now said she doesn’t identify with the label.

Others using the hashtag on their content say the same.

We chat to Crystal Gorsuch, who is 20 and a stay-at-home mum. What does she think of the label and how has her content been received by people online?

Plus, Chelsea from the team talks to us about how this trend is changing and where it might go next.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討許多社群創作者拒絕被貼上「傳統妻子」 tradwife 標籤的現象。主持人 Hannah Gelbart 與 BBC 記者 Chelsea Coates 訪問了 20 歲的全職媽媽 Krystalle Gorsuch ，並討論 Nara Smith 與 Hannah Neeleman 等熱門創作者。許多創作者雖然會使用相關標籤來提高影片曝光率，但並不認同該稱呼，強調自己並非 1950 年代缺乏權利的傳統主婦，而是擁有成功事業與商業影響力的女性。節目亦剖析了此趨勢背後的政治爭議、極端企圖，以及在 18 至 24 歲年輕族群間的影響與發展前景。
summaryEn: This episode of BBC's What in the World examines why popular stay-at-home mothers and social media influencers are rejecting the "tradwife" (traditional wife) label. Host Hannah Gelbart and BBC journalist Chelsea Coates speak with 20-year-old stay-at-home mum Krystalle Gorsuch and discuss high-profile creators like Nara Smith and Hannah Neeleman (Ballerina Farm). Although many influencers use tradwife hashtags to boost content views, they reject the label itself, emphasizing that they are not powerless 1950s housewives, but successful businesswomen running profitable digital platforms. The episode also explores the political controversies, criticisms of hypocrisy, and strong appeal of this trend among audiences aged 18 to 24.

phrases.example: So, their definition is a married woman, especially one who posts on social media, who stays at home doing cooking, cleaning, etc., and has children that she takes care of.
I started posting when I first found out I was pregnant.
So, I continued posting, continued building a community, in hopes that my social media could help support us while we both took unpaid leaves after our daughter was born, and it really took off.
I think, literally speaking, that term comes from just a place of unacceptance, a place of, I almost want to say, hatred for women who choose to stay at home.
So, I mentioned Nara Smith earlier, but another one of the most popular accounts that people tend to refer to as a tradwife account is Hannah Neeleman's account.

vocabulary.example: But in recent years, that kind of definition has broadened.
But recently there's been kind of controversy and backlash related to it because of an interview that Nara Smith did.
About halfway through my pregnancy, my husband and I had to relocate, and he had to get a new job.
And because of that normalization, when a woman chooses to do something different, then it's just like, oh, what are you doing?
They have huge followings on social media, which they monetize.
They haven't admitted that they're proponents of themselves.
Some of the videos I've seen are actually like parody videos, quite satirical, they're laughing at the kind of the concept.
And we know that the more emotive content people post, the more divisive it is, often the more engagement it gets.

But I have to say that some people, or a lot of the followers, you said Hannah Neeleman's got 10 million followers on on Instagram, they find her stuff really aspirational because on the face of it, it's a woman who gets to live this beautiful lifestyle without having to work a 9-to-5 in an office.
So, I think we are going to see that kind of idea endure for a much longer time.
